title: A hedge round the orchard
hook: defending Guru Hargobind's new ways, Bhai Gurdas says an orchard needs a thorny hedge (Bhai Gurdas, Var 26)

segments.voice: Yesterday, one, two, five, and your line, where five gather. Did you ask two people to sit with you? Day seven hundred eleven.

Nobody plants a hedge of thorns for its own sake. Thorn bushes aren't pretty, and they snag your sleeve. But walk around an old orchard, with fruit hanging low and goats wandering nearby, and the thorns suddenly make sense. They were never there for themselves. They were there for the fruit. Bhai Gurdas reached for exactly that picture when people were troubled by a Guru who didn't look like the Gurus before him. Today: kikar.
screen: `NOBODY PLANTS THORNS FOR FUN.` → `AN ORCHARD, AND GOATS NEARBY.` → `A GURU WHO LOOKED DIFFERENT.`

segments.voice: The Guru was Guru Hargobind. Sikh tradition remembers him as the Guru who took up the sword alongside the Guru's word, and kept horses and armed Sikhs around him. And some people didn't like it. In his twenty-sixth var, Bhai Gurdas sets out what they were saying, and he doesn't soften it. The earlier Gurus sat in the dharamsal, they said, and this one doesn't stay in one place. He keeps dogs. He goes hunting. The Gurus before him gave us hymns; this one doesn't sit and compose them. It's a list of complaints, and Bhai Gurdas lets it stand in full. Then he answers. The truth, he says, can't be hidden, and the Sikhs still gather round the Guru like bees round a lotus. And then the picture that names today. To protect an orchard, you plant a hedge of thorny kikar around it. The hedge isn't the orchard. It isn't the fruit. Nobody walks into an orchard to admire the thorns. But without them, the fruit doesn't survive the season. Hear what Bhai Gurdas is claiming. The swords and horses aren't a change of heart. The orchard is the same one Nanak planted: the Name, the sangat, the Guru's word. The hedge is what keeps it alive in hard times. That's a careful argument, and it holds two things together that people tend to pull apart. Gentleness and protection. A path of humility, and the readiness to defend it. Sikhs speak of this as miri and piri, the worldly and the spiritual held by the same Guru. Bhai Gurdas says it with a gardener's eye.
screen: `A GURU WITH SWORD AND HORSES.` · `THE COMPLAINTS, IN FULL.` · `A HEDGE OF THORNY KIKAR.` · `THE HEDGE IS NOT THE ORCHARD.` · then, large: `A HEDGE FOR THE ORCHARD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: protect one good thing. Use the sit to name it. Something growing in your life that's easy to trample. A morning routine. A friendship that's still new. A child's bedtime story. An hour that's supposed to be yours. Then ask what would keep it safe. Not a wall. A hedge. A small boundary: a phone left in another room, a no said kindly, a time written down. Choose one, and decide where it goes. If you pray, you can say Waheguru over the thing you're guarding. The bell holds the time.
Kikar, the thorny tree Bhai Gurdas pictures hedging an orchard: the orchard needs it to keep the fruit alive, answering those troubled by Guru Hargobind's new ways.
Your line: a hedge for the orchard. Today, plant the one small boundary you chose, and notice what grows behind it. Day seven hundred eleven.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember Guru Hargobind for holding miri and piri together, worldly and spiritual authority, and Bhai Gurdas's twenty-sixth var is read as an early defense of that change.

notes: Var 26 pauri 24 paraphrased from memory: the complaints (earlier Gurus sat in the dharamsal, this one doesn't stay in one place; keeps dogs; goes hunting; does not compose/sing bani as before) and the reply (truth can't be hidden; Sikhs like bees on the lotus; a hedge of kikar round the orchard).
